title: Becanus: kind- and small-matter venials perfectly against law if deliberate
source_text: XXX. Et quidem dicit esse perfecte contra legem peccata venialia ex suo genere; ut risum immodicum, & verbum otiosum, & etiam venialia ex parvitate materiae, ut furtum rei exigui momenti; si talia peccata deliberate fiant. Peccata vero quae venialia sunt ex defectu perfectae deliberationis, quales sunt subiti & indeliberati motus irae, odii, invidiae, superbiae, luxuriae, &c. esse imperfecte contra legem: ut exempli gratia, motum indeliberatum concupiscentiae esse imperfecte contra legem illam Decalogi, Non concupisces.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed he says that venial sins from their own kind are perfectly against the law—as immoderate laughter and an idle word—and also venials from smallness of matter, as theft of a thing of slight moment, if such sins are done deliberately. But sins which are venial from defect of perfect deliberation—such as sudden and indeliberate motions of anger, hatred, envy, pride, lust, and so on—are imperfectly against the law: as, for example, an indeliberate motion of concupiscence is imperfectly against that law of the Decalogue, You shall not covet.
pass_b_english: Deliberate kind-venials and small-matter thefts Becanus counts as perfectly against the law.
Sudden indeliberate motions are only imperfectly against precepts like ‘You shall not covet.’
